title: Diatonic Answers: An Explainer
content_blocks: This one is for the musicians out there who already understand what a fugue is and how it works, and want to know more about what I do differently.

Every presentation of the subject in a fugue is called an ‘entry’ or an ‘entrance’. Traditionally, the second entrance of the subject is called the ‘answer’. There are two different types of answers: real answers, which are precise transpositions of the subject, and tonal answers, which are slightly-modified transpositions of the subject, in order to stay closer to the original key (and to help achieve the scale degree 1↔︎5 swap that is supposed to happen with a fugue answer). With the exception of the slight modifications in tonal answers, though, the basic melodic structure of answers are always precisely what they are in the subjects: melodic steps are answered by melodic steps, and larger leaps are answered by correspondingly-larger leaps.

Since intervals in some of my newly-devised modes—including the one I wrote about yesterday—change, though, transposing the subject up or down will change the character of the melody, sometimes dramatically so. I call this a diatonic answer: the scale pattern remains identical with the original subject, but the intervals from one note to another are changed. I use this technique in many other fugues in both sets.
